content:
Artificial intelligence company Anthropic said Thursday that it had successfully thwarted a number of potential conspiracies this year in which scientists were using its AI model for research that could be used to develop biological weapons.

In a new report detailing misuse of its AI models — which it said is rare — Anthropic published five case studies showing scientists using its models in ways that could help advance bioweapons development. Those actors "circumvented our restrictions designed to prevent users from accessing our models from unsupported locations, and used other means to conceal their research purposes in order to evade our safety guardrails," the company said.

"When we detected and investigated these cases, we banned the relevant user accounts and incorporated the findings into our frontier model safeguards, law enforcement, and threat intelligence workflows with the aim of better preventing, detecting, and disrupting similar activity in the future," Anthropic said in the report.

The company did not disclose the names of the research institutions involved, the countries they were in, or the specific biological agents involved. Anthropic could not determine whether the research was for legitimate purposes or malicious intent, since genuine scientific inquiry that could lead to medical breakthroughs could also potentially lead to the creation of dangerous modified pathogens.

"Sophisticated threat actors are aware that we ... are working to detect dangerous uses of our models, and they exploit the dual-use nature of biology to create a 'reasonable deniability' around their research," the report said.

"As a result, clear malicious intent is often instead a sign that an actor is not particularly sophisticated. The more sophisticated actors can conceal their intent, seeking help from our models in ways that appear reasonable and constructive on the surface, but when analyzed in aggregate show clear signs of misuse. It is these sorts of interactions we are reporting on," the report added.

"Sophisticated actors are aware that we ... are working to detect dangerous uses of our models, and they exploit the dual-use nature of biology to create a 'reasonable deniability' around their research." — Anthropic

One case involved a scientist who turned to Anthropic's AI chatbot, Claude, in May for help drafting a grant application to fund research on chikungunya, a virus spread by Aedes mosquitoes. While such research could ultimately contribute to vaccine development, in this case the scientist wanted to engineer mutations in the virus to make it more harmful when repeatedly infecting live animals, Anthropic said.

"We are inclined to think that this research was not entirely benign, in part because the institutional context of the grant itself is concerning. While the information in the application suggests the research is conducted by civilian researchers, the intent was actually to conduct it within a military research institute," the report said.

Anthropic's report also touched on misuse of its AI models in cyberattacks, surveillance, and building conventional weapons. But while much of the public attention has focused on the cyberattack threats of AI and its potential to misalign with human intentions, experts have expressed concern about its potential for bioweapons misuse.

Andrew Weber, a senior fellow at the Council on Strategic Risks, told the New York Times that the Anthropic case studies were "chilling examples of state-sponsored bioweapons developers leveraging the rapidly advancing capabilities of frontier AI models."

The report comes as multiple Anthropic employees have publicly raised safety and existential risks from AI. A former researcher at the company previously warned that AI companies are "racing headlong into self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
